title_en: Zhang Yanjuan v. Jiangsu Wanhua Industry & Trade Development Co., Ltd., Wan Hua, Wu Liangliang, and Mao Jianwei — dispute over shareholder rights
ruling_gist_en: 1. A limited liability company shall convene a shareholders meeting and adopt meeting resolutions in accordance with the relevant provisions of the law and the company's articles of association. If a shareholders meeting is not convened and resolutions are not adopted according to law, but instead the shareholder who actually controls the company fabricates the shareholders meeting and its resolutions, even if such shareholder actually holds the vast majority of shares and corresponding voting rights in the company, his individual decision cannot replace the validity of the shareholders' resolution. Under such circumstances, if other shareholders apply to confirm the invalidity of the fabricated shareholders meeting and its resolutions, the people's court shall support such application.
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over shareholder rights; First instance; Basic People's Court; Jiangsu Province; Natural person; Legal person; Company Law; Validity of shareholders' resolution; Validity of equity transfer agreement; Statute of limitations; Support plaintiff; Fabricated shareholders' resolution; Equity transfer; Confirmation of shareholder qualification; Shareholder rights; Mao Jianwei shareholder rights dispute
full_text_en:
Zhang Yanjuan v. Jiangsu Wanhua Industry & Trade Development Co., Ltd., Wan Hua, Wu Liangliang, and Mao Jianwei — Dispute over Shareholders' Rights

[Ruling Summary]

1. A limited liability company's convening of a shareholders' meeting and the making of meeting resolutions shall be conducted in accordance with the provisions of the law and the company's articles of association. Where a shareholders' meeting is not lawfully convened and a resolution is not lawfully made, but rather a shareholder who actually controls the company fabricates a shareholders' meeting and its resolutions, even if that shareholder actually holds the vast majority of the company's shares and corresponding voting rights, his or her individual decision cannot substitute for the effect of a shareholders' meeting resolution. In such circumstances, where other shareholders apply for a declaration that the fabricated shareholders' meeting and its resolutions are invalid, the people's court shall support such application.

2. The provision in Article 22 of the revised Company Law, which states that "where the convening procedures or voting methods of a shareholders' meeting, general meeting, or board of directors' meeting violate laws, administrative regulations, or the company's articles of association, or the content of a resolution violates the company's articles of association, a shareholder may, within sixty days from the date the resolution is made, request the people's court to revoke it," is a provision made for shareholders' meetings that are actually convened and the resolutions made thereat. That is, in such circumstances, the shareholder must request the people's court to revoke the resolution within sixty days from the date the resolution is made; failure to do so within the time limit will result in no support. However, with regard to the aforementioned fabricated shareholders' meetings and their resolutions, as long as other shareholders file a lawsuit within the statute of limitations prescribed by law after knowing or should have known that their shareholder rights were infringed, the people's court shall accept the case according to law, and is not subject to the restriction of the sixty-day period under Article 22 of the revised Company Law concerning a shareholder's application to revoke a shareholders' meeting resolution.

Plaintiff: Zhang Yanjuan, female, 42 years old, technician at Jiangsu Coal Geophysical Surveying Team, residing at Chengxian Street, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Jiangsu Wanhua Industry & Trade Development Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. 116 Hongwu North Road, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Legal Representative: Wu Liangliang.

Defendant: Wan Hua, male, 41 years old, director of Jiangsu Wanhua Industry & Trade Development Co., Ltd., residing at Guojiashan, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, husband of plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan.

Defendant: Wu Liangliang, female, 27 years old, residing at Hongwu North Road, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Mao Jianwei, male, 51 years old, salesman of Nanjing Xuefang Commercial Center, residing at Baiguoshu, Baixia District, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan filed a lawsuit with Xuanwu District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, due to a dispute over shareholders' rights with defendants Jiangsu Wanhua Industry & Trade Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Wanhua Industry & Trade Company), Wan Hua, Wu Liangliang, and Mao Jianwei.

Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan alleged: Defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company was established in 1995 with a registered capital of RMB 1,060,000. The incorporators were defendant Wan Hua (plaintiff's husband), plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan, and two other shareholders, Zhu Yuqian and Shen Long. Among them, Wan Hua contributed RMB 1,000,000, and each of the three shareholders, including Zhang Yanjuan, contributed RMB 20,000. In June 2006, when the plaintiff, for some reason, checked the business registration records, she discovered that the shareholders and legal representative of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company had been changed as early as April 2004. The plaintiff, Zhu Yuqian, and Shen Long were no longer shareholders of the company, the plaintiff's equity had been transferred to defendant Mao Jianwei, and Wan Hua had also transferred the company equity corresponding to RMB 800,000 of his RMB 1,000,000 contribution to defendant Wu Liangliang, and the company's legal representative had been changed from Wan Hua to Wu Liangliang. The basis for Wanhua Industry & Trade Company to make the above changes was the resolution of the Wanhua Industry & Trade Company shareholders' meeting held on April 6, 2004. However, the plaintiff, as a shareholder of the company, was never notified to attend that shareholders' meeting, never transferred her own equity, and never saw the resolution of that meeting. The signatures of the plaintiff on the resolution of that shareholders' meeting and the capital contribution transfer agreements were not written by the plaintiff herself. Therefore, the plaintiff believed that the shareholders' meeting was not actually convened, and the meeting resolution and capital contribution transfer agreements were all false and invalid, infringing upon the plaintiff's lawful shareholder rights and interests. The plaintiff neither transferred her own equity nor agreed to Wan Hua's transfer of equity to persons other than the company's shareholders. Wan Hua is the plaintiff's husband, but he was cohabiting with Wu Liangliang. The equity transfer between them was actually a transfer of community property, without a genuine transaction. The equity transfer between Wan Hua and Wu Liangliang also violated the provision of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company's articles of association that "shareholders shall not transfer equity to persons other than shareholders," and did not inform other shareholders or obtain the consent of other shareholders as required by Wanhua Industry & Trade Company's articles of association. Therefore, the plaintiff requested the court to confirm that the so-called April 6, 2004, Wanhua Industry & Trade Company shareholders' meeting resolution was invalid, confirm that the equity transfer agreement between the plaintiff and Mao Jianwei was invalid, confirm that the equity transfer agreement between Wan Hua and Wu Liangliang was invalid, or alternatively, revoke the aforesaid shareholders' meeting resolution and equity transfer agreements.

Defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company argued: The content of the shareholders' meeting resolution passed by Wanhua Industry & Trade Company on April 6, 2004, did not violate the law. Former shareholders Zhu Yuqian and Shen Long of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company were both aware of the content of that shareholders' meeting resolution and the fact of the equity transfer. Therefore, the resolution was lawful and valid. Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan claimed that she did not receive the meeting notice and did not attend that shareholders' meeting. Even if her claim were established, it could only mean that the procedures for the April 6, 2004, Wanhua Industry & Trade Company shareholders' meeting did not comply with the law and the company's articles of association. Article 22 of the revised *Company Law of the People's Republic of China* (hereinafter referred to as the Company Law) provides: Where the convening procedures or voting methods of a shareholders' meeting, general meeting, or board of directors' meeting violate laws, administrative regulations, or the company's articles of association, or the content of a resolution violates the company's articles of association, a shareholder may, within 60 days from the date the resolution is made, request the people's court to revoke it. At the time the plaintiff filed the lawsuit, the 60-day legal period for applying to revoke the resolution had already expired. Therefore, the April 6, 2004, Wanhua Industry & Trade Company shareholders' meeting resolution had already taken effect. The plaintiff had no right to deny the effect of that shareholders' meeting resolution. Furthermore, the plaintiff was not a proper plaintiff in this case because, as of April 6, 2004, all of the plaintiff's equity had been transferred to defendant Mao Jianwei, and the plaintiff was no longer a shareholder. Therefore, she had no right to initiate this lawsuit. The defendant requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

Defendant Wan Hua argued: The shareholders' meeting of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company held on April 6, 2004, was lawful. I enjoyed all voting rights in Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, and the shareholders' meeting resolution passed with my consent should be valid. The transfer of the company equity corresponding to my personal contribution of RMB 800,000 to defendant Wu Liangliang was consented to by all shareholders of the company. Therefore, the transfer was also valid. Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan alleged that she did not attend the shareholders' meeting and did not sign the relevant documents; this is true. However, because I and the plaintiff are husband and wife and our property is commingled, and we had previously agreed that the company equity belonged to me, my attendance at the shareholders' meeting on behalf of the plaintiff and my signing on her behalf in the shareholders' meeting resolution and equity transfer agreement were both lawful and valid. As of April 6, 2004, the plaintiff was no longer a shareholder of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company and had no right to initiate this lawsuit.

Defendant Wu Liangliang argued: As the transferee of the equity, I should not be a defendant in this case. The procedure for my acquisition of the equity was lawful. Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan and defendant Wan Hua are husband and wife. I had reason to believe that Wan Hua could represent the plaintiff in expressing a waiver of her preemptive right to purchase Wan Hua's equity. Even if the plaintiff did not authorize Wan Hua to express a waiver of the preemptive right, as a bona fide purchaser, my lawful rights and interests should be protected. The marital dispute between the plaintiff and Wan Hua should be dealt with in accordance with the Marriage Law and has nothing to do with me. The April 6, 2004, shareholders' meeting resolution and capital contribution transfer agreement of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company should all be deemed valid. I acquired the equity and was elected as the chairman of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company more than two years ago. The company has been operating normally, and during this period, the plaintiff has never raised any claim that the shareholders' meeting resolution was illegal or infringing. On April 6, 2004, I purchased part of Wan Hua's equity in Wanhua Industry & Trade Company at a price of RMB 800,000. If the plaintiff or Wan Hua is willing to acquire the equity at the same price now, I agree to transfer the equity back to the plaintiff or Wan Hua.

Defendant Mao Jianwei argued: Defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company once borrowed my ID card, but I was completely unaware that I had acquired the equity of plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan and others in Wanhua Industry & Trade Company. I never attended the April 6, 2004, Wanhua Industry & Trade Company shareholders' meeting, and I do not know the company's shareholders Shen Long, Zhu Yuqian, or others. The signature of Mao Jianwei on Wanhua Industry & Trade Company's articles of association, the April 6, 2004, shareholders' meeting resolution, and the equity transfer agreements was not written by me.

Facts Found by the Court at First Instance (Xuanwu District People's Court of Nanjing):

Defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company was established on December 21, 1995. The incorporators were defendant Wan Hua, plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan, and two other shareholders, Zhu Yuqian and Shen Long. The registered capital was RMB 1,060,000, of which Wan Hua contributed RMB 1,000,000, and each of Zhu Yuqian, Shen Long, and Zhang Yanjuan contributed RMB 20,000. On November 23, 1995, Wan Hua, Zhu Yuqian, Shen Long, and Zhang Yanjuan signed the articles of association of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company. The articles of association stipulated, among other things: Shareholders of the company shall not transfer their equity to persons other than shareholders; they may only transfer among themselves, but this must be consented to by all shareholders; shareholders have the preemptive right to purchase equity transferred by other shareholders; at shareholders' meetings, shareholders shall exercise voting rights in proportion to their capital contributions, with each RMB 100,000 constituting one voting right; shareholders' meetings are divided into regular meetings and extraordinary meetings, and all shareholders shall be notified five days prior to the convening of a meeting; regular shareholders' meetings shall be held once a month; shareholders may also attend shareholders' meetings by proxy in writing, exercising the rights specified in the power of attorney; shareholders' meetings shall make resolutions on the matters discussed, and resolutions shall be passed by shareholders representing more than one-half of the voting rights; resolutions on matters such as increasing or decreasing registered capital, transferring equity, merger, division, change of company form, dissolution, liquidation, etc., shall be passed by shareholders representing two-thirds or more of the voting rights; minutes of the decisions on matters discussed at shareholders' meetings shall be made, and shareholders present at the meeting shall sign the minutes, etc.

After the establishment of defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, defendant Wan Hua was responsible for the company's operation and management.

On April 12, 2004, defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company applied to the company registration authority for registration of changes, specifically: (1) changing the company name to Jiangsu Office Partner Trading Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Partner Trading Company); (2) changing the legal representative to defendant Wu Liangliang, and changing the shareholders to the four persons: defendant Wan Hua, Wu Liangliang, Mao Jianwei, and shareholder Xing Xiaoying; (3) amending certain parts of the company's articles of association.

The materials on which defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company relied to apply for the above registration of changes were:

1. Two equity transfer agreements dated April 6, 2004. Their main contents were: Defendant Wan Hua transferred the company equity corresponding to RMB 800,000 of his RMB 1,000,000 contribution to defendant Wu Liangliang; Zhu Yuqian transferred the company equity corresponding to his RMB 20,000 contribution to Xing Xiaoying; Shen Long transferred the equity corresponding to RMB 10,000 of his RMB 20,000 contribution to defendant Mao Jianwei, and the equity corresponding to the other RMB 10,000 to Xing Xiaoying; plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan transferred the company equity corresponding to her RMB 20,000 contribution to Mao Jianwei. The above two equity transfer agreements bore the signatures of all transferors and transferees at the foot.

2. One amended version of the articles of association of defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company (Revised on April 6, 2004). In addition to recording and confirming the changes concerning the company's shareholders, directors, supervisors, domicile, and name, the articles of association also stipulated, among other things: Company shareholders have the right to attend shareholders' meetings, exercise voting rights in proportion to their capital contributions, vote for the company's directors or supervisors, and enjoy the right to be elected; company shareholders have the right to transfer their capital contributions in accordance with the law and the company's articles of association; a shareholder transferring equity to a person other than a shareholder must obtain the consent of more than half of the shareholders, and dissenting shareholders shall purchase the equity to be transferred; if they do not purchase the equity, they are deemed to consent to the transfer to a person other than a shareholder; for equity transferred with the consent of the company's shareholders, other shareholders have the preemptive right to purchase such equity on equal terms; after a shareholder lawfully transfers equity, the company shall prepare a new register of shareholders; shareholders' meetings are divided into regular meetings and extraordinary meetings; regular meetings shall be held once a year; extraordinary meetings may be convened upon the proposal of shareholders representing one-fourth or more of the voting rights, or one-third of the directors or supervisors; shareholders attending a shareholders' meeting may also appoint a proxy in writing to attend the meeting and exercise the rights specified in the power of attorney; to convene a shareholders' meeting, all shareholders shall be notified in writing 15 days prior to the meeting; the shareholders' meeting shall make minutes of the decisions on matters discussed, and shareholders present at the meeting shall sign the minutes, etc. This amended version of the articles of association bore the signatures of defendants Wu Liangliang, Mao Jianwei, Wan Hua, and shareholder Xing Xiaoying.

3. One copy of the shareholders' meeting resolution of defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company dated April 6, 2004. Its main contents were: All shareholders unanimously agreed to the above equity transfers; after the transfers, the capital contributions of each shareholder and their proportions of the registered capital were: defendant Wu Liangliang contributed RMB 800,000, accounting for 75.5%; defendant Wan Hua contributed RMB 200,000, accounting for 18.9%; Xing Xiaoying contributed RMB 30,000, accounting for 2.8%; defendant Mao Jianwei contributed RMB 30,000, accounting for 2.8%; all shareholders unanimously agreed to change the company name to "Jiangsu Office Partner Trading Development Co., Ltd."; all shareholders unanimously agreed to change the company's domicile to "No. 116 Hongwu North Road, Nanjing"; all shareholders unanimously agreed to remove Zhu Yuqian and Shen Long from their positions as directors and re-elect Wu Liangliang and Mao Jianwei as directors to form a board of directors with Wan Hua; all shareholders unanimously agreed to remove plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan from her position as supervisor and elect Xing Xiaoying as supervisor; all shareholders unanimously agreed to the company's articles of association as amended on April 6, 2004.

It was also found that plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan and defendant Wan Hua were married in 1988 and are currently husband and wife.

The above facts were confirmed by evidence including the articles of association of defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, the equity transfer agreements dated April 6, 2004, the shareholders' meeting resolution dated April 6, 2004, the amended articles of association of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company (Revised on April 6, 2004), the industrial and commercial registration files, a certificate from the Qixia District Archives of Nanjing, and the court trial records.

In addition, during the first-instance trial, the parties also submitted or requested the court to collect the following evidence regarding the relevant facts of the case:

Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan provided investigation records of witnesses Zhang Jun, Ding Houyu, and Wan Neng, among others, to prove that defendant Wan Hua and defendant Wu Liangliang had cohabited and addressed each other as husband and wife, and that Wan Hua had used property of defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company to purchase real estate and vehicles for Wu Liangliang. It also proved that Zhang Yanjuan and Wan Hua had previously agreed to divorce in 1999, and Zhang Yanjuan had received RMB 300,000 based on a divorce agreement with Wan Hua, and then in 2000, she had given the RMB 300,000 back to Wanhua Industry & Trade Company. Regarding this, Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, Wan Hua, and Wu Liangliang all argued that the three witnesses Zhang Jun, Ding Houyu, and Wan Neng had not appeared in court to testify, so the truthfulness and legality of their testimony could not be confirmed. Defendant Mao Jianwei argued that this evidence was unrelated to him.

Upon the application of plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan, Xuanwu District People's Court of Nanjing conducted an investigation into Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian, shareholders of defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company. Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian stated: When Wanhua Industry & Trade Company was established in 1995, we two, at the request of defendant Wan Hua and plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan (a married couple), acted as nominal shareholders of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company. In fact, neither of us made any capital contribution, and we never participated in the operation of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company afterward. Neither of us received a notice for the April 6, 2004, Wanhua Industry & Trade Company shareholders' meeting; we did not attend that shareholders' meeting; the signatures of Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian on the equity transfer agreements and the shareholders' meeting resolution in question were not written by us. We did not know Xing Xiaoying and Mao Jianwei, the transferees of the equity, and we did not receive any consideration for the transfer of equity. Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian also stated that they did not wish to become involved in the marital dispute between Zhang Yanjuan and Wan Hua, and how the equity of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company registered under their names was handled was unrelated to them. Regarding this, Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, Wan Hua, and defendant Wu Liangliang argued that in April 2004, Wanhua Industry & Trade Company notified Zhu Yuqian, Shen Long, Xing Xiaoying, and defendant Mao Jianwei to attend the Wanhua Industry & Trade Company shareholders' meeting on April 6 of that year, and that Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian attended that shareholders' meeting and signed the shareholders' meeting resolution and equity transfer agreements. Apart from this, the other statements made by Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian were true.

Defendants Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, Wan Hua, and Wu Liangliang provided a divorce agreement signed by Wan Hua and plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan on March 12, 1999. The agreement stipulated: Zhang Yanjuan and Wan Hua agreed to divorce due to incompatibility; all tangible and intangible assets, creditor's rights, and debts of the couple in Wanhua Industry & Trade Company belonged entirely to Wan Hua; the property due to Zhang Yanjuan was calculated at RMB 700,000, to be paid by Wan Hua in installments. They also provided a payment certificate issued by Zhang Yanjuan on March 12, 1999, proving that Zhang Yanjuan had received RMB 300,000 paid by Wan Hua under the divorce agreement. Based on the above evidence, Wan Hua argued that although he and Zhang Yanjuan were husband and wife, they had already made a division of their property. All property of the couple in Wanhua Industry & Trade Company belonged to Wan Hua. Therefore, Wan Hua had the right to dispose of his equity in Wanhua Industry & Trade Company and also had the right to dispose of the equity corresponding to Zhang Yanjuan's RMB 20,000 contribution. Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, Wan Hua, and Wu Liangliang also provided two powers of attorney issued by Shen Long, Zhu Yuqian, and Zhang Yanjuan in November 1995, authorizing Wan Hua to collect their personal share subscription funds and handle matters such as the registration of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company. Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, Wan Hua, and Wu Liangliang argued based on these powers of attorney that Wan Hua had always handled company affairs on behalf of Zhang Yanjuan, and Zhang Yanjuan had always accepted this. Zhang Yanjuan did not dispute the authenticity of the above evidence, but argued that the divorce agreement was an agreement between her and Wan Hua for the purpose of divorce, including property division content. Since the parties signed that divorce agreement in March 1999 but have not yet divorced to date, the divorce agreement has not taken effect. Wan Hua once paid Zhang Yanjuan RMB 300,000, but later, for some reason, Zhang Yanjuan returned the money to Wan Hua, as witnessed by Zhang Jun, Ding Houyu, and others present. As for the two powers of attorney issued by Shen Long, Zhu Yuqian, and Zhang Yanjuan in November 1995 authorizing Wan Hua to collect personal share subscription funds and handle matters such as the registration of Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, these precisely demonstrate that Zhang Yanjuan's authorization for Wan Hua to handle company affairs required a written power of attorney. However, Wan Hua's transfer of Zhang Yanjuan's equity on April 6, 2004, was made without Zhang Yanjuan's power of attorney, indicating that Wan Hua's action was not authorized by Zhang Yanjuan. Therefore, the transfer should be deemed invalid.

Defendant Mao Jianwei argued that the above evidence was all unrelated to him.

During the first-instance trial, defendant Wanhua Industry & Trade Company supplemented its statement: The shareholders' meeting on April 6, 2004, had minutes, which bore the signatures of all attendees. However, it failed to provide the minutes of that meeting as required by the first-instance court. Furthermore, because witnesses Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian and defendant Mao Jianwei all denied signing the equity transfer agreements and the shareholders' meeting resolution in question, the first-instance court asked defendants Wanhua Industry & Trade Company, Wan Hua, and Wu Liangliang whether they wished to apply for a forensic examination of the authenticity of the signatures of Shen Long, Zhu Yuqian, and Mao Jianwei on the said equity transfer agreements and shareholders' meeting resolution. All three defendants stated that they would not apply for such an examination.

Regarding the evidence submitted by both parties as set forth above, the court of first instance reviewed and concluded as follows:

1.  Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan did not object to the divorce agreement and one certificate signed by her and Defendant Wanhua on March 12, 1999, nor to the two powers of attorney issued by Shen Long, Zhu Yuqian, and Zhang Yanjuan in November 1995. The court confirmed the authenticity, legality, and relevance of the aforementioned evidence to the facts of this case, and it may serve as the basis for deciding the case.

2.  With respect to the testimony of witnesses Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian, because Shen Long and Zhu Yuqian were shareholders of Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., their statements concerned the disputed facts of this case. As these two witnesses were unable to testify in court due to objective reasons, the court, upon the plaintiff's application and in accordance with the provisions of the Supreme People's Court's *Several Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings*, collected their testimony. The court confirmed the legality and relevance of their testimony. Except for the part where Defendants Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., Wanhua, and Wu Liangliang raised objections to the witnesses' statements denying their participation in the shareholders' meeting on April 6, 2004, and their signing of the shareholders' meeting resolution and the equity transfer agreement, the defendants affirmed the other contents of the statements made by these two witnesses. Although the three defendants claimed that the two witnesses had signed the shareholders' meeting resolution and the equity transfer agreement, and asserted that a meeting record existed for the shareholders' meeting of April 6, 2004, which bore the signatures of the attendees, they failed to apply for a handwriting comparison of the signatures on the shareholders' meeting resolution and the equity transfer agreement after the witnesses denied signing them. They also failed to provide relevant evidence such as the shareholders' meeting record to support their claim. Therefore, the court also confirmed the authenticity of the aforementioned witness testimony.

3.  Regarding the interview records with witnesses Zhang Jun, Ding Houyu, and Wan Neng provided by the plaintiff, upon examination, it was found that these interview records were prepared by the plaintiff's agent ad litem. None of the aforementioned three witnesses testified in court. Therefore, the court did not confirm the authenticity of the testimony of these three witnesses, and it cannot be used as evidence for deciding this case.

In summary, regarding the facts asserted by both parties based on the above evidence, the court of first instance finds:

The divorce agreement was an agreement reached between Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan and Defendant Wanhua concerning the divorce of the couple and the division of property after divorce. After the divorce agreement was signed, Zhang Yanjuan and Wanhua did not actually go through with the divorce, so the provisions regarding the division of property after divorce within that agreement have no effect. Wanhua's claim, based on the divorce agreement, that he is entitled to all rights of the couple in Defendant Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., lacks sufficient evidence and is not accepted by the court.

The two powers of attorney issued by Zhu Yuqian, Shen Long, and Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan to Defendant Wanhua in November 1995 specified and detailed the authorized matters. These documents can prove that Zhu Yuqian, Shen Long, and Zhang Yanjuan once authorized Wanhua in writing to handle certain company affairs, but they cannot prove that Zhang Yanjuan authorized Wanhua to transfer her equity in Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. In the absence of other corroborating evidence, Wanhua's claim that he had the right to transfer Zhang Yanjuan's equity on her behalf cannot be established.

Defendants Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., Wanhua, and Wu Liangliang claimed that Zhu Yuqian and Shen Long attended the shareholders' meeting of Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. on April 6, 2004, and signed the shareholders' meeting resolution and the equity transfer agreement from that meeting. However, aside from the shareholders' meeting resolution and the equity transfer agreement themselves, the defendants failed to provide other evidence to prove this. The testimony of Zhu Yuqian and Shen Long, as well as the statements of Defendant Mao Jianwei, are consistent with each other and contradict the defendants' claims. Based on the existing evidence in this case, it cannot be determined that Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. notified Shen Long, Zhu Yuqian, and Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan to attend the shareholders' meeting on April 6, 2004. Nor can it be determined that Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. convened a shareholders' meeting on April 6, 2004, attended by Wanhua, Zhang Yanjuan, Shen Long, and Zhu Yuqian. Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., Wanhua, and Wu Liangliang also failed to provide evidence to prove that a shareholders' meeting resolution jointly signed by Wanhua, Shen Long, Zhu Yuqian, and Zhang Yanjuan was formed on April 6, 2004, or that Shen Long, Zhu Yuqian, Zhang Yanjuan, Xing Xiaoying, and Defendant Mao Jianwei jointly signed the equity transfer agreement on April 6, 2004.

The focal issues of dispute in this case are: First, whether the shareholders' meeting resolution made by Defendant Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. on April 6, 2004, and the involved equity transfer agreement are valid; Second, whether Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan's application for a declaration of invalidity or revocation of the aforementioned shareholders' meeting resolution and equity transfer agreement should be supported.

The Xuanwu District People's Court of Nanjing City held in the first instance:

A shareholders' meeting of a limited liability company shall be convened by a convener who meets the legal requirements, following the procedures stipulated by law or the company's articles of association, summoning all shareholders to attend, and shall be presided over by a chairperson who meets the legal requirements. When the shareholders' meeting needs to make resolutions on relevant matters, shareholders shall deliberate in accordance with the methods of discussion and voting procedures stipulated by law or the company's articles of association. A shareholders' meeting resolution can be formed only when the proportion of voting rights required by law or the company's articles of association is reached. When a limited liability company makes resolutions through a shareholders' meeting on matters such as amending the company's articles of association or deciding on equity transfers, the essence is a process in which the company's shareholders exercise their shareholder rights by participating in the shareholders' meeting and decide to change their civil legal relationships with the company. Therefore, the actual participation of the company's shareholders in the shareholders' meeting and the expression of their true intentions are necessary conditions for the validity of the shareholders' meeting and its resolutions. In this case, although Defendant Wanhua held an absolute majority of voting rights in Defendant Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., this does not mean that Wanhua's personal decision-making process, facilitated by his control over the company, is equivalent to having convened a company shareholders' meeting. Nor does it mean that Wanhua's personal will can replace the effect of a shareholders' meeting resolution. Based on the facts of this case, it cannot be determined that Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. actually convened a shareholders' meeting on April 6, 2004, and it is even less possible to determine that a genuine and valid shareholders' meeting resolution was formed from that meeting. The so-called "shareholders' meeting resolution" relied upon by Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. to decide on matters such as handling company registration changes and equity transfers was fabricated by Wanhua, who was then the controller of the company. It did not actually exist, and therefore, it naturally cannot have legal effect.

Defendants Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., Wanhua, and Wu Liangliang argued that Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan's lawsuit exceeded the 60-day period stipulated in Article 22 of the revised *Company Law* for applying to revoke a shareholders' meeting resolution, and therefore, her claims should not be supported. Regarding this argument, the court held that this case occurred before the revision of the *Company Law* and should be governed by the legal provisions in effect at that time. Given that Article 22 of the revised *Company Law* allows shareholders to file an action for a declaration of invalidity or an application for revocation of a shareholders' meeting resolution, whereas the pre-revision *Company Law* did not have clear provisions on related issues, this case may refer to and apply the provisions of Article 22 of the revised *Company Law* in accordance with Article 2 of the Supreme People's Court's *Several Provisions on the Application of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (I)*. However, Article 22 of the revised *Company Law* stipulates that "if the convening procedures or voting methods of a shareholders' meeting, general meeting of shareholders, or board of directors violate laws, administrative regulations, or the company's articles of association, or if the content of the resolution violates the company's articles of association, shareholders may, within 60 days from the date the resolution is made, request the people's court to revoke it." This provision is specifically addressed to actually convened company shareholders' meetings and the resolutions made therein. In such cases, shareholders must request revocation by the people's court within 60 days from the date the shareholders' meeting resolution is made; failure to do so will result in no support for the request. In the present case, the shareholders' meeting of Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. on April 6, 2004, and its resolution did not actually exist. As long as the plaintiff files a lawsuit within the statutory statute of limitations after knowing or should have known that her shareholder rights were infringed, the people's court shall accept the case according to law, and it is not bound by the 60-day limit stipulated in Article 22 of the revised *Company Law* for shareholders applying to revoke a shareholders' meeting resolution.

A shareholder's transfer of equity to other shareholders or to persons outside the company is a civil contractual act based on consensus between the shareholder (equity transferor) and the equity transferee. One of the prerequisites for the formation of such a contract is that both parties have a genuine intention to transfer and accept the equity. In this case, it cannot be determined that Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan and Defendant Mao Jianwei actually signed an equity transfer agreement. Nor can it be determined that Defendant Wanhua had the authority to represent Zhang Yanjuan in transferring the equity. Mao Jianwei neither paid actual consideration for accepting Zhang Yanjuan's equity nor had any intention to accept Zhang Yanjuan's equity. He was even entirely unaware that he had accepted the equity of Zhang Yanjuan and others. During the litigation, he explicitly stated that he would not ratify this fact. Therefore, the equity transfer agreement cannot be established according to law. Consequently, the claims of Defendants Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., Wanhua, and Wu Liangliang that Zhang Yanjuan was no longer a shareholder of Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. and thus could not initiate this lawsuit cannot be established and are not supported by law.

Regarding the equity transfer agreement signed between Defendant Wanhua and Wu Liangliang, according to the relevant provisions of the pre-revision *Company Law* and the articles of association of Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd., where a shareholder transfers equity to a person outside the company, the consent of more than half of all shareholders is required. In this case, Wanhua's transfer of equity to Wu Liangliang was neither notified to the other shareholders nor, more importantly, consented to by more than half of all shareholders. Therefore, this equity transfer act is invalid.

In conclusion, the Xuanwu District People's Court of Nanjing City, pursuant to Article 64, Paragraph 1, and Article 128 of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, Article 57 of the *General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China*, Article 35, Paragraph 2, Article 37, Article 39, Article 40, Article 41, Article 43, and Article 44 of the pre-revision *Company Law*, and Article 1 of the Supreme People's Court's *Several Provisions on the Application of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (I)*, rendered the following judgment on April 2, 2007:

I. The shareholders' meeting resolution of Defendant Wanhua Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. dated April 6, 2004, is not established.

II. The equity transfer agreement between Plaintiff Zhang Yanjuan and Defendant Mao Jianwei dated April 6, 2004, is not established.

III. The equity transfer agreement between Defendant Wanhua and Defendant Wu Liangliang dated April 6, 2004, is invalid.

After the judgment of the first instance was pronounced, none of the parties filed an appeal within the statutory period, and the judgment of the first instance has taken legal effect.
